title: Dana Paramita
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of approaching others' actions with generosity and intellectual empathy, recognizing that we don't have all the information and that our understanding is limited by our own perspectives. This involves going beyond forgiveness to cultivate a more open-minded and compassionate approach, drawing on Buddhist teachings such as the paramitas and "Buddha-like" intentions. By cultivating this mindset through meditation and perfection of concentration, we can develop a greater sense of calm and non-judgmental awareness in daily life, allowing us to embody bodhisattva qualities such as loving kindness and letting go of harm.

sentences.text: Hello again and welcome to the people online.

I am recognizing today as I try to have a dharma talk that is prepared but not overprepared, and then events in the world happen, and I am not sure where they fit in, but I want to acknowledge that, local and global.

We have another weekend bombing campaign, and then I heard the name of our Wilderness Dharma partner, Luba, on the memorial service, which is new to me, and we will just feel into that and really take the opportunity to ask or to look at the big questions of why we are here, what are we doing here.
First, there is the big three: suffering, old age, and death.
That is the big question, and that is the focus of Buddhism and Zen, and the other one is compassion, and so everything we practice is really a focus on those.
We will jump in and see where that lands.
I worked on the President's Day holiday.

It was scheduled to be a holiday, but I worked at the hospital, and there is a skeleton crew there that day, and some minor issues came up, so I was looking around at who was available to direct around to address them.
I looked at the calendar, and it showed that everybody was here today, which I knew wasn't true, and it was frustrating.
In fact, I was a bit angry at the person who was supposed to be doing the scheduling because now I don't know who to talk to.
Then the thoughts arose of, "Well, gee, it just doesn't understand the seriousness of us having this information about who to call," and maybe a little bit lazy.

Then I came to find out that the names had all been updated on the schedule, but it was a new version of the schedule because toward the last minute I had asked for a new version of the schedule to be created, and there probably would have been time to get it out on the Friday, except that I asked him to take on a couple of other projects.
Looking at these assumed intentions, we will carry that into the topic of today.
We have been studying the paramitas, and Razala has already done a talk on Donna Paramita, but as Chris said last week, it is our favorite one.
So I want to look at really a very specific element of generosity.

I had an insight into this element of generosity with a philosophy paper that I wrote in college that I thought I had done a really excellent job, a strong argument of just totally skewering the argument that I was going to make.

I thought I had done a really excellent job, a strong argument of just totally skewering the author of the paper that I was reviewing, and the professor came back and said, "Well, everything you said was correct, but you weren't taking the generous interpretation of what he was saying."

That in debate maybe you go for, or in law you go for whatever you can, but the intention here is that we try to understand their argument as well as we could possibly have made it if we were trying to make that argument.
So what I want to look at today is generosity in our interpretations of others' actions, generosity in our assumptions about intentions.
This goes beyond forgiveness, and forgiveness is highly recommended.
Forgiveness is challenging.
Forgiveness has a lot of resources in Zen; it is something that we talk about that it comes up through the years of our study.
It encourages us to seek out our blind spots and our confusions and recognize that everyone is acting out of blind spots and confusions.
But I want to go beyond forgiveness to actually recognizing that we do not know everything.
That is kind of another core Zen principle: questioning what it is that we think we know, and especially when it comes to other people.

Chris also mentioned the Dale Wright book on the Paramitas is the old standby book, so when I was thinking about doing this talk, I got out my old Dale Wright book on the Paramitas, and ironically, I was surprised to find just how much lack of generosity I had toward Dale Wright in reading it because the book was just peppered with these comments on what he wrote, like, "This isn't right," and "He doesn't understand the Dharma."
Oh, that was probably fifteen years ago that I was reading that.
Yes, he understands a little more now, right?
We take that from our perspective up, approaching the whole of life as the whole of life as both, and in the moment, what am I experiencing?
What am I experiencing?
And a recognition that the separation is a delusion.
In our meal chant, we talk about the three wheels: giver, receiver, and gift.

And maybe when we are looking at interpreting what the actions and the statements of others are, we could perform a similar—there is the giver, receiver, and gift, there is the me, the you, and what we are talking about.
And when it comes to others, there is no separation between myself and the person who I believe is wrong and whatever it is that I think they are wrong about.
Now we wrap in generosity to that, this effort to reach out with doing a little bit more, reach out with a little energy to explore that.
As mentioned plenty, I have mentioned a few times that we are a, this is a practice of lists.
We have all the lists, so the four unlimited emotions are loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, compassion, and equanimity.
And this also does not quite fit in there, or maybe this is a specific application of that.
There is something missing, which is this, and we will call it an intellectual empathy.
That the empathy is being able to feel from the perspective of the other person, and a piece of that is being able to think from the perspective of the other person.

Of course, we have to start with generosity focused inward, as I think about how we often mess that up with feeling guilt in a non-productive way, that is just pain that is basically just violence to ourselves.
So all of the studying that we are doing is within that context of what makes the world a better place and is not just violence to ourselves.

Maybe another step besides forgiveness on the path to trying to look at the intentions of others is the Buddhist practice of imagining that everything that anybody else in the world does is because they are a Buddha and they are doing it for your benefit.
This is a practice I learned about from Jack Kornfield in his book, *Path with Heart*, which is just a carrying on of ancient teachings.
Boy, imagine that.
Every time you get caught off in traffic, anytime somebody says a rumor about you, it is for your benefit.
That is a wonderful practice to put us in the mindset.

And that is also not quite what I am talking about because we do that practice purely to focus on the benefit of it and not really believing that they are doing it because they are a Buddha for my benefit.
So we keep studying.
The quote from Nancy Mujo Baker said, "Notice the moralistic connotation of these words.
These words being that somebody else is wrong, that somebody else is at fault.
An assumption that things or people should be other than what they are.
Notice the should here.
When we find fault, not only do we have a preference, but we are ready to reject something, to exclude it from our world and definitely from ourselves.
Often what we think of as faults may not be at all, especially when whatever it is is not harming others, and it is just something I reject in myself."
Thank God I do not have her elbows.
Although I think a lot of times we have perceptions about what is harming others or is harming me, and all of it feeds our mistaken notions of separateness.

I think the paramitas, the precepts, appreciated Hannah's job of tying the perfections back to the precepts, back to our ethical work, and looking at how that is founded on that fundamental flaw in our perception that there is separateness.
We are having a two-for-one special today, so I also want to talk about another paramita just so we do not have too much generosity.
And I did not want us to go through this whole series of talks without hitting dhyana, perfection of concentration, or meditation.
Meditation is the better translation.

Dhyana was, actually, I am not sure, I did not verify whether that is a Sanskrit or a Pali word, probably Sanskrit, but through hundreds of years of teaching, that word dhyana became Chan, Chinese Chan, which then became in Japan Zen.
So the very name of this practice is that perfection of meditation.
And that word, sometimes as we read the paramitas, is translated as the perfection of concentration, but in the original teachings, it did not mean that.

They very clearly chose the word that was the practice of meditation, the practice of sitting down with intention to do nothing, well, sitting down with intention to do whatever it is that we do in meditation.
And not on the benefits that arise from it or concentrate, you know, those other words.
And yet, ironically, our practice, which took that as the name, flipped it on its head and brought it back to mean the practice of all of it with Dogen's teachings, that everything is meditation.
So it is, for us, the perfection of bringing all of our lives, everything we do, to be this effort that we are practicing in meditation.
So, meditation, going back, let us just start.
I was caught today in our grass-roof hermitage as we chanted that on the Just Return, so that got me thinking about returning, and which is that is our meditation.
So we start with our good posture, and we sit in meditation.
I want to cover a few of those points in meditation because that is what that perfection is.

We sit with our, if we are on our cushion and then we can get on the chair or whatever, but we sit with our hips rolled forward a little bit, maybe definitely our back straight unless we have some, all of our bodies are different.
Most of us are able to maintain the straight back, and that is highly encouraged if we can make that part of our meditation so that as though we are suspended from the top of our head.

And as we are putting all of this effort into that posture, we cannot let go of the effort of letting it go, of letting the shoulders fall down, of not holding the tension in our hips, of really finding that balance point so that we do not have to put a bunch of extra muscle work into it.
So starting with that point of posture, we bring our mind to whatever it is that we have chosen as our focus.
Oftentimes our breath, bring our mind to our breath, bring our mind to our next breath.
And then we realize that we are not bringing our mind to our breath, that we are somewhere else.
So then we return.
That is step four, right, is always that returning, that coming back to it.
And that does not just apply on the cushion.
That applies to our steps every day.
Norman Fischer, and the world could be otherwise, points that out.
Zen's approach to meditation is set: everything is meditation, or nothing is but meditation.
Meditation is beyond meditation, so there is no need to meditate.
Insight is sudden, constant, all pervasive, and therefore unnecessary.
How do we come to this profoundly liberative understanding?
By practicing meditation so that we can understand how useless it is.
Isn't that typical Norman?
And by continuing to practice meditation, not because it is necessary or even helpful, but because we are bodhisattvas who are dedicated to sharing practice with others.
It transcends life and death, purity and impurity.

And then the little piece from Norman that just captures it so much for me, the irony of what we are trying to do: meditation is a process of returning to our true selves that know that we are nothing other than everything we are not.
Our true selves that know that we are nothing other than everything we are not.
That separation does not exist, and of course it does.
We have to get the fork to our mouth.
We have to deal with getting up every day and going to work, but we also need to see that lack of separation.
I appreciate it again in Chris's talk last week, and I do not have the exact words, but something like serenity does not mean that it all stops whirling.
The world continues whirling around us.
And then of course it is not like we are sitting as the calm with everything going around us.
We are part of the whirling too.
But when we get to our true selves, that is the calm in the middle.
So back a bit to looking at others' intentions with generosity, and with the particularly challenging for many of us, time for that is when we are looking at what is going on in politics.
Do we so readily reach the conclusion that half of the population of America is purely selfish, unethical, or suckers?
We get into this habit often from my experience of talking with people and listening to people of very quickly villainizing.
So let us come back to looking at our relationship on the precept of not expounding on the faults of others, a practice recommended by Kathleen Shokai Bishop.
Begin by deciding how you will completely relinquish yourself to the life of the Bodhisattva in thoughts, words, and actions.
Step one.
Step two.
Set your intention to be mindful of words of harm to self or others.
Step three.
Accept the Buddha's boundless loving-kindness in each situation.

And step four, finally, this is for the practice of the precept, the journal, but explicitly note how we are learning to embody the truth, that truth of non-separation, and all of its aspects, thoughts, words, and actions that are affecting our life.
And good luck with that.
In the study of the precepts, Rich and I are studying the opening to *Oneness* book by Nancy Muchot Baker as part of our preparation for marriage in a few months, which is delightful.
And I cannot imagine a better study for marriage than to be looking at our ethical stance together and really looking at our own faults together.
I especially appreciate in that book, in the opening to *Oneness*, the new-to-me interpretation of the absolute.

We have long talked about the precepts as being seen from a literal understanding, like we just follow it because it says that, a relative understanding, recognizing that sometimes just following the words does not quite do the job, absolute understanding being the standpoint of non-separateness.
And what Nancy Muchot Baker adds to that discussion is an emphasis on that the precepts arise naturally as we have encounters with clear seeing.
That it is not about don't just following a rule, but it is about what arises naturally as we recognize our unity with others.
The book, *Opening to Oneness*, is becoming one, and that is particularly relevant in that getting married, right?
We are becoming one, so there is a little bit more to that Oneness.
And so the last note of that, I hope that everybody here will be able to join us in celebrating that marriage with a potluck after our sit on June 7th.
So, please, please come on June 7th and join us.
That is Sunday here.
Let us do some exercise.
So, actually I guess we could, maybe, I do not know, do we keep the recording going while I walk us through?
Let us, yeah, maybe we can keep the recording going until we get to the point of discussion.

We will be continuing the discussion.
